utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Josse, I think there are two items on the agenda before we continue with the examination-in-chief of Mr. Poplasen. The first, although I do not know any details, is that there was a translation issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If I could deal with that first, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I sent an e-mail to offices of the Chamber this morning. I asked them not to send it to the Judges because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, we have not -- I do understand that you have provided an alternative translation. I have been informed that there was an issue of translation and that the Defence considered an alternative translation better, but I haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Simply because I wanted the agreement of my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think we've agreed this much -- I can hand it up, although they haven't as yet agreed or commented upon the translation I'm about to hand up. It's short. It relates to Article 3 of the decision that we spent a lot of time on yesterday, so I've got plenty of copies here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, could you please assist Mr. Josse. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can tell you our position on this. We have received communications from the Defence in respect to this proposed re-translation. We have some issues with it. We will -- we have shown it to our language assistants. We will be in touch with the Defence and we will see if we can find a resolution as to an agreed-upon translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I see that there are some differences. I notice that "war commissioner" now reads "war delegation."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's nuance, Your Honour, rather than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- markedly different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I suggest that -- of course, if the parties would agree on the translation, the Chamber, if it comes down to translations, would not fully rely on an agreement between the parties, because the Chamber would like to have this checked through the services of the CLSS. But if the parties would agree on what would be the most appropriate translation, we could send that for review to the CLSS and see -- see what the final result will be. When do the parties think they could agree on ... Because the witness is now here, I would rather not wait for ages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Perhaps we can submit this issue on Monday, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but then I would -- I would first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As I said, it's fine if the parties agree on this, but that's not the most important matter. I will ask CLSS whether they could compare the translation suggested by the Defence team with the translation as has been provided and to give whatever comment they'd like to give, if that would be possible. We're talking about six or seven lines. I take it that there must be a possibility that someone reviews these seven lines, because it's only Article 3, from what I understand, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I don't know -- Mr. Registrar, perhaps you could assist us in making already contact because it's not a -- I don't know exactly how you divide your work, the -- those who are translating written text I think is a different group from those who are assisting us during the -- during the hearings. Mr. Registrar, may I take it that you give these three -- we are talking about a B/C/S original, the translation provided by the Prosecution, and the alternative translation suggested by the Defence, that it will be in the hands of the CLSS and that we hear as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this -- this is a document that was used yesterday, was it, with the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Then I would not have suggested Monday because I was not privy to the discussions with Mr. Josse about this. I thought this was something that didn't have such an urgent nature. If I had known, I would not have made that suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, of course you have the material there as well. So if everyone works on it, these seven lines, we would know as soon as possible what would be the most reliable translation, and it still is language, and translation is a complex matter, as we are aware of. Then the next issue was, Mr. Josse, you asked for five minutes to orally argue the admissibility of the Savkic exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. Could I, before my five minutes begin, deal with the issue of provenance, because quite a lot has happened about that since the last occasion the matter was aired in court. As the Court is aware, Mr. Margetts sent an e-mail first to the Defence and then to the Chamber, detailing the provenance of all these documents. Having considered the matter, the Defence accept what is contained within that e-mail; however, the issue so far as P1055 and P1056 is concerned remains slightly unresolved. And in the course of the last 24 hours - indeed it may actually only be today, to be fair - I have made some further inquiries of Mr. Margetts because, Your Honour, the position is that 1055, that was the first document that I objected to, that was the one that the witness said was a forgery. It transpires that apparently it was obtained from the archives of the Boksit company in Milici. Well, unsurprisingly, that was of some real interest to the Defence, bearing in mind what the witness was saying and bearing in mind how the witness -- the issue of forgery. So some further inquiries have been made and I would invite Mr. Margetts to inform the Chamber about them and then perhaps we could see how they can be entered effectively into the evidence, because the Defence want these matters as part of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. There was the document where the witness testified, I think, that it was in the interest of the Boksit company to have something on paper --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely. And in re-examination I asked him who it was who forged them and he basically said it was Serbs within that organisation, that's who he guessed had been responsible for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But perhaps Mr. Margetts could give the extra information because, as I say, I'm very anxious that that be on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, first of all in regard to the provenance and the e-mail we sent of 23 February, and it was subsequently forwarded to the Trial Chamber, this is how we described the provenance of that document: It was part of a group of documents delivered to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 29th of October, 2002, by the liaison officer of the Republika Srpska government, Mr. Trifun Jovicic, and he informed the OTP that the documents were obtained from the archives of the Boksit company in Milici. My learned friend made some further inquiries and asked whether we could provide some further information in relation to that. We did so today, an e-mail to my learned friend, and this is the information we provided: The provision of these documents and a number of other documents to the OTP arose from an interview that was conducted with Mr. Rajko Dukic in Belgrade on the 1st of September, 2002. I - referring to myself, Stephen Margetts - participated in that interview. And during the course of that interview, Rajko Dukic undertook to provide documents related to paragraph 2 of Exhibit P52 to us. And Your Honours will recall Exhibit P52; it's the facsimile dated 15th December, 1992, sent to Mr. Krajisnik and addressed to Mr. Karadzic. And in paragraph 2, it refers to approximately a little bit more than 3 million Deutschmarks aid provided to Republika Srpska, and it refers to the characterisation of that as a tax liability. So that's the further information that we've provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I just add this: I then asked Mr. Margetts this question in writing: "Are you saying that Dukic provided these documents to Jovicic?" And he provided with the answer: "Correct."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can confirm that that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And though I have said to Mr. Margetts that I invite the Prosecution to make further inquiries, I think for the purpose of this argument that isn't necessary. It's quite clear to the Chamber that the Prosecution accept that it was Mr. Dukic himself who provided them to the liaison officer, who then passed them on to the Office of the Prosecutor. Your Honour, these are my submissions: The issue of these documents raises, in our submission, a number of interesting and important questions. Could I begin by endorsing, in effect, what Your Honour put to Mr. Margetts in the course of argument on the 23rd of February, when, at page 20816 of the transcript, Your Honour in effect said insofar as a forgery is concerned, and this related to P1055: "Does a forgery -- if it's true that it's a forgery, this document could well be understood as corroborating the witness's evidence that the Crisis Staff never existed because documents that are produced are forgeries. If, however, it very much depends on whether it's a forgery, yes or no. If it's a forgery, then it might support the witness's views. If not, well, it's likely to corroborate the Prosecution's view." And then a moment later Your Honour said: "But is it for the witness to demonstrate that it's a forgery or is it for the Prosecution to demonstrate that it's an authentic document?" Well, Your Honour, the Defence say that it's for the Prosecution to prove that it's not a forgery and to prove that beyond a reasonable doubt. And it's important to do things in the correct order because clearly that is of some relevance. So far as Mr. Margetts's submissions that then followed on the 23rd of February are concerned, we contend that they were ostensibly misconceived. He classically put the cart before the horse. In effect, so far as virtually, if not every document, he invites admission of the document on the basis that the Trial Chamber can conclude that the witness is lying. This is not a helpful approach, in our submission, because it can't be proper or helpful for a party objecting to the admissibility of their document from the other party to make a long speech commenting on why the witness is not telling the truth. In passing, we contend, that it's slightly surprising that the Trial Chamber didn't stop Mr. Margetts. Having said that, what it does mean is that if Mr. Margetts's approach is correct, the basis of admission would necessarily entail, in relation to any document objected, the Trial Chamber making all sorts of findings about the witness, firstly, before deciding if the document should be admitted into evidence at all; and secondly, of course, before the end of the case and before hearing all of the evidence. So Mr. Margetts's approach is fundamentally flawed, in our submission. Your Honour, if the Defence have got this particular hare running, if I can mix my metaphors, by raising the objection, then we apologise, but we repeat submissions that have been made earlier in this case that the parameters as to the use and admission of documents in this case is, in our contention, far too inconsistent and occasions wooly. It's not in the interests of justice, we contend, nor in the interests of proper time management to approach the matter in this slightly haphazard fashion. I can assist to this regard -- extent, Your Honour, having said what I have just contended: Having looked at what Mr. Margetts has said, I withdraw our objection so far as P1059 and P1060 are concerned, but maintain the objection so far as the other documents. So far as P1055 is concerned, the Chamber is now faced with, we contend, a difficult exercise. The witness says the document's a forgery. There isn't a jot of evidence to rebut what he says, we contend. Supposing the Court says: Well, the Prosecution haven't proved it's not a forgery. Double negative on my part because of course the burden is on them. What should then happen? Should it be admitted? Well, if it's not admitted, then what happens to that part of the transcript that deals with the cross-examination and re-examination in relation to that document? That part of the transcript would be meaningless if the document isn't admitted, and it's also rather important in relation to the context of the witness's evidence as a whole. If it is admitted, P1055, how can the Court seriously justify, we submit, stopping the Defence, for example, trying to adduce documents that come from a book or from any other source? In short, if a forgery is admitted into evidence, or a document that might be a forgery, then surely anything can be admitted in evidence. We contend that the Court should have some proper, equally applied filtration system so that the parties are able to deal with the matter on a consistent basis. Finally, if the Court says: Well, we'll wait -- we'll admit the document and we'll wait and see until the end of the case what weight to attach to it, the Chamber, we submit, will then be committing itself to making specific findings in relation to each and every document that has been put in evidence in the course of this trial. Your Honour, I accept that the submissions I've just made raise some important issues, but we submit they are the natural consequence of what I say, with the greatest respect, is an ultra liberal approach to the admission of evidence in this courtroom. Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you a few questions, Mr. Josse. Would you agree with me that whether or not it makes sense to admit forged documents also depends on the issue which should be -- or the facts that should be proved? For example, I can imagine that if you want to prosecute someone for forging documents, a forged document could well be admitted into evidence as proof of the forgery.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you would agree with me that it does depend on what you intend to prove. Let's just assume -- I'm putting it to you in order that your answer could assist the Chamber to take the right decisions. Let's just assume that the fact that Crisis Staff documents would be forged to -- in the interest of private parties, would the Defence support admission into evidence of such a forged document in order to strengthen the Defence case that forged documents were produced at that time for reasons such as promoting the interest of third parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In those circumstances, quite possibly. I mean, I concede, thinking aloud, that it's possible that, had we known of the existence of the document, it's possible we might have put it to him for him - Savkic, giving the specific example - to have said this is a forgery and trying to have it admitted on that basis. I accept that that's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's of course one of the options --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- because you say why -- if you would admit a forged document, then of course every book should be admitted as well. I think it's -- there are more nuances in the problem. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then -- now I invite both parties to comment on it. Is it possible at all that one would admit a document for both reasons; the Defence because it wants to demonstrate that forged documents were produced at the time and then, since this witness says it is a forged document, that this is material evidence of that, whereas the Prosecution says this proves that the witness is not telling us the truth because it -- he tries to -- he tries to hide -- or he tries to escape a problem he is faced with, that is, that documents prove something which is not in accordance with his testimony up till that moment. I mean, I'm just -- I put it to you as an open question whether it's imaginable that admission into evidence could finally result in either a finding, if it is at all necessary to make a specific finding on this aspect, which would -- could result in favouring the Defence case or favouring the Prosecution's case. I mean, if we do not admit it, Mr. Josse, you also exclude a favourable explanation of this document for the Defence. I'm -- should that be clear on from the beginning, should we admit it only for this and this purpose, as we have done sometimes, or should we keep it open in this case? It's not entirely clear to me yet what we should do. Of course, the Judges together will have to decide that, but I'm just asking your opinion about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, if I -- if I'm being invited to make a submission on the point, the Defence contend that the proper approach would be to exclude the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then accept that we have no objective basis in the document itself anymore on using it in support of the evidence given by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have no answer to, for example, what one then does with the lengthy passages in the transcript that deal with the document and which, in many ways, act as a foundation for what then comes afterwards. That is a real problem. That is the filtration process that I was referring to. Your Honour, this is, with respect -- isn't a criticism at all. I didn't have very long. This is a very big issue. This trial has been going on for an extremely long period of time, and I basically raised some thoughts and submissions that have crossed my mind. That's how I would like to put it, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may do so. I'll first give an opportunity to Mr. Margetts to respond to my question and how happy he would be if finally the admission into evidence of this document would result in a finding that it is a forgery and that the witness, therefore, was not lying but was speaking the truth, to put it just as sharp as I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The answer to Your Honour's question is a simple yes, we consider that this specific document and documents of this category should be entered into evidence and then ultimately the Court will go to weigh these documents and go to weigh the evidence of the witness and come to a conclusion in relation to the reliability of the document and possibly a related conclusion in relation to the credibility and reliability of the evidence of the witness. And this document, in effect, doesn't really fall into a different category than any other document that's admitted before the Court. The Court may make adverse or favourable findings in regard to any document, regardless if whether it's a specific allegation of forgery or not. So there would be our responses to Your Honour's question, that documents of this nature should be admitted into evidence. I did have one matter of clarification I wanted to make in regard to Mr. Josse's submissions but I may leave that to an opportunity Your Honour may or may not give me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'll give you that opportunity, but I'd first like to put another question to Mr. Josse. Mr. Josse, if, for the better understanding of the transcript, even if you would not admit the document into evidence, of course another way is to mark it for identification so that at least it's there and if ever an Appeals Chamber would have to look at it, they could at least see what we discussed. Is that a solution which you would be in favour of? Because you seem to be very much inclined to say it should not be admitted, but this practical problem would be overcome by not admitting it but by marking it for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That seems a sensible approach, with respect, bearing in mind some of the practical difficulties that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I suggest the following to both parties: Perhaps you were surprised by the questions put by the Bench. I'd like to give you another 48 hours to consider whether there's any further need, and then again it would be just as short as it was now, as brief, that you have an opportunity to give any further, well, let's say not more than two or three minutes, and, Mr. Margetts, would it be a suggestion that we first wait and see whether Mr. Josse uses this opportunity and then you add any further comment? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that would be suitable. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, so two days from -- well, let's say two hearing days, which means that if we would not sit -- 48 hours would end at the weekend; that's not an appropriate moment. Let's say the -- at the first hearing after this weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Josse, are you ready to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- continue the examination of Mr. Poplasen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Poplasen. You had to wait for a while. First of all we had a late start because the morning session ended late; second we had to deal with a procedural matter. So our apologies for the time you had to wait. May I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Josse, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, yesterday we concluded with your reminding the Chamber that you had set up your own political party in 1993, but you began putting it together in 1992. And you, in the course of your evidence, had given quite a long explanation as to differences between how your party, the Serb Radical Party, and the SDS saw various issues. I don't want to go back over those matters. What I do want to ask you about is when in 1992 you started driving around Bosnia, forming your political party, what was it in terms of what you had seen in Pale that made you decide that really another political party needed to run the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are many questions there. One of them has to do with chronology, in a way, and the other deals with some general issues relating to the political reasons for the formation of the party. I just wish to make several preliminary observations. It is true that the inaugural session of the Assembly of the Serb Radical Party was held in March 1993 in Banja Luka and that this was formally the start of the party as an organisation covering practically the entire Republika Srpska. However, in practical terms, the work of the party had started much earlier. According to our regulations - I don't remember at this time what sort of regulations were in place, whether we needed 50 or 100 signatures by citizens in order for a party to be registered with a court - but at any rate we did this as early as in 1992. The fact that the party had been registered with a court in 1992 meant that it already had several boards numbering 50-odd people. It was enough for the party to have several boards for it to be registered. Sometime in the summer of 1992 we registered the party with the court in Ilidza. This is one of the municipalities under Sarajevo. This was, in fact, confirmed in a court decision and some other documents. Next, we -- several of us; there was me, there was a commissioner from Ilidza, and the commissioner from Ilijas -- embarked on this effort of touring different municipalities and establishing boards. And in March 1993 -- or rather, by March 1993, we had established Municipal Boards of the Radical Party. At the same time in Serbia, the Serbian Radical Party had a very influential say and was becoming ever more popular. It was from such a situation that our political reasons were derived. We believed that we lived in an area where the Serbs ought to continue living in one community. And when I say "community," I do not mean -- I did not mean a single state. The ties could be cultural, economic, educational, and so on and so forth, whereas the political organisation in a territory always depends on some general conditions. For instance, the Serbs from Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state could be fully integrated into this cultural, educational, informational, and so on and so forth structure with the Serbs in Serbia without, in fact, living in the same state. The -- as far as we were concerned, we knew that the issue of the establishment of a state did not depend on us but on the events at large. However, we continued insisting on this building-up of ties. If possible, in terms of a state; if not, then any other ties. Yesterday, in response to some of the questions, I stated that the SDS had gave up the idea. And I have to reiterate here that when I say that the SDS gave it up, I'm not referring to a specific session or any meeting of the Serbian Democratic Party where this was decided, but rather it was our inference that this was the position of the SDS on the basis of some concrete steps taken by the leadership of the SDS. Now I'm turning to your question as to which reasons compelled us to establish the Serbian Radical Party. In our conviction, we wanted to build up ties with the Serb majority population in those areas where the Serb people's representatives were elected. These were the areas with the majority Serb population in Bosnia-Herzegovina, including the territories with the Serb majority in the Republic of Croatia and Montenegro. I have to point out that following the inaugural session in March 1993, whenever I had the chance to, I exerted strong pressure on the leadership of the Republika Srpska, including Mr. Krajisnik -- or perhaps on Mr. Krajisnik in particular, because under the state system it is the parliament where different suggestions and opinions and positions are gathered and are then discussed. It is true that we were not a parliamentary party, but in politics there are other ways of dealing with this. There are opinion polls which indicated clearly that we enjoyed popularity. The Serbian Radical Party in Serbia was very successful; it won one-third of seats in the elections in 1992 in the Republic of Serbia and was thus the second strongest party. This is a matter or a question for some other people, including Mr. Krajisnik. One of these initiatives of mine - perhaps the motives were somewhat different, but I cannot say that, it was for those who were deciding to say that - was to adopt -- to have a declaration adopted by the parliament of the Republika Srpska to unite with the Republic of the Serbian Krajina. I'm telling you what I remember about it, and I stand corrected if I say something wrong. After I had suggested to Mr. Krajisnik that this step be taken, he told me: Well, why don't you draft the first version of it? I took one night to draft the entire text of the declaration, and I sent it to Mr. Krajisnik, I handed it to Mr. Krajisnik. Several days later, I don't know how many, there was the session of the Assembly of Republika Srpska in Prijedor, and later on, from some documentation, I saw that this declaration was included into the textbook on the constitutional right -- on the constitutional law. So this was one of the matters on which made us indecisive. We didn't know whether to in fact support the SDS or whether to attack it, because there was this matter. Because the SDS policy was contrary to our policies, we did not support it, but I gave you an illustration of why we, nevertheless, continued supporting the SDS. The other reason why we criticised and distanced ourselves from the SDS was the emergence of crime and corruption in the Republika Srpska. I do not wish to say that there was less crime or corruption to be found in the other war-affected areas or, for that matter, that there was less crime even in the countries that were not caught in the -- in a war. I believe that there are countries that were not in a war but still suffer from crime which -- and corruption. Of course there are different definitions of crime, so that's why we can put it this way. What we objected to, in fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In fact, I would like you - perhaps you were about to do it - to define what you mean by crime and corruption.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me, I'd first like to say why I was mentioning crime, and what I wanted to say was that it can, in fact, be legalised crime, but I will explain it in the following way. I'm just giving you an illustration, of course. If highly developed Western countries, including the USA, purchase large amounts of oil from Middle East and then pay in dollars - I'm just giving you a general example, I'm not referring to any dates or anything - and then the New York banks increase their interest rates by several percentages, compared to the other banks in -- worldwide, those who sold the fuel deposit their monies in the New York banks. In this way the US of A has both fuel and the money. As a result, the profit they gained would then be invested at interest rates that would be much lower than the ones existing in their bank. Ultimately, raw materials in general, fuel included, and the money end up in the Western countries and the investments into the underdeveloped countries, including those that have fuel resources, are used up to patch the whole matter up to make it seem legal and to make it seem in keeping with the world trade relations under a system which keeps a good part of the world in poverty. This is what I meant to say when I was referring to this large system of injustice. Now, moving away from this large system of injustice, which is not a topic here, let's look at the properties that were damaged in the places where there was no war. There were dead people there. There was dissatisfaction among the people. Many people dodged mobilisation. There were these minor instances of injustice that were dispersed which could be called crime and corruption which we objected to because they had an impact on the morale of the fighters, of the population, and so on and so forth. We also raised these matters purely for propaganda reasons. People were dissatisfied with the existence of the crime; we pointed our finger to the SDS that was in power and that was responsible for that. And of course the dissatisfaction is in -- is channeled to those who seem to be exponents of the crime. So this was also part of our political propaganda and of our anticipation that the elections were forthcoming. The third reason why we distanced ourself from the SDS and set up our own party was that we estimated that the SDS became more and more obedient and lent its ear to some messages coming from the outside. And I'm referring to a number of mediators, special representatives of the United Nations, representatives of the European Community, and so on and so forth, but I'm also referring to the pressure exerted from Belgrade. I did not take part in these conversations. I met Mr. Milosevic in 1997. I had never met him before. There were these persons who came to Bosnia and placed an obstacle to the realisation of our policies. As a result, we found ourselves in a position where occasionally we supported the Serbian Democratic Party whenever we assessed it to be in keeping with our policies, and occasionally we would criticise the party and its steps quite harshly. I don't know if I've been too extensive in my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, perhaps, but either way I don't have any follow-up questions on this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't know whether Your Honour does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It took quite some time to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- hear this course of political economics and then, at the same time - because that's what I understand was the purpose of it all - to emphasise the independent approach from this witness and his party-to-be.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's right. I mean, my question quite --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have no follow-up questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any need, I give you one hour to consider whether it's really -- whether we really need further explanations. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like briefly, Mr. Poplasen, to return to what we were -- what you were giving evidence about yesterday in relation to your job as a commissioner. You described how you liaised with Mr. Koljevic in the Presidency. Did you have any liaison with the government in the course of your work as a commissioner?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commissioners were both commissioners of the Presidency and the government. I know that the then-Deputy Prime Minister Milan Trbojevic was charged with following the work of the commissioners on behalf of the government. I had one conversation with him which had to do with our activity, and he promised that they would do whatever was within their power to do. The government was relocated from Pale, and subsequently I only addressed the government in writing, but I did not have any direct contacts with Mr. Trbojevic anymore with regard to our work. I had regular contacts with Professor Koljevic, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Before we move away, so to speak, from Pale, you have described how you were in what I will call, using a colloquial English expression, the corridors of power for the short time in 1992. I would like you, please, to make an assessment of some of the people you rubbed shoulders with there and their influence, as far as you were concerned, with events and how they controlled events. Firstly, Radovan Karadzic, please.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, numerous social and psychological studies of the populations of the Balkans indicate something that should be noted here. Mr. Karadzic hailed from the Dinara area which has this typical mind-set which is quite violent. So this is not just typical of him, it is rather typical of the area, and there is general agreement about this. I mention this because I wish to say that Mr. Karadzic was a typical representative of this mind-set characterised by large ideas and ambitions, more interested in visions than in practical problems. As far as I could observe, he dealt with practical problems away quite quickly, without much hesitation, which of course opens the possibility of error. However, unlike other persons in critical situations in times of crisis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, you were asked about influence and control of events. You're giving us a -- at least you started giving us a general impression of the personality of Mr. Karadzic and how he dealt with matters in more general terms, but would you please focus on the question first. And Mr. Josse then would like to know what was his influence; and second, how did he control, if he did, events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Considering such characteristics, I could not claim with any certainty that in the first months, the early days, March, April, May, Mr. Karadzic had very firm control of the events. I believe that this became more prominent at a later stage, both his influence and his control. This is my assessment, however. I'm -- did not have an opportunity or did not analyse it at the time. However, I believe that his influence was important and -- and decisive. Since there were other violent characters such as General Malic there as well, inevitably conflicts emerged for persons -- between persons of similar character, and I believe this had quite a bearing on the situation. The other persons in the leadership of Republika Srpska were, however, of a different character. They were -- their character was not similar to that of Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about Mr. Koljevic. Now you've told us that he was a person you knew by far and away best, that he was the person you worked with. In particular, a specific question about him: Could you assess his skills as a politician.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Koljevic was, first of all, a good man, a humanitarian, and an idealist, who, however, did not have much talent for politics. I cannot say that he had any political skills, but, at any rate, if he had any potential skills for politics, they did not manifest themselves. What he did in political terms was not much or was not even adequate for the political role he held, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about Mrs. Plavsic? I'd like you to assess her power and her skills as a politician, please, both.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Mrs. Plavsic, I had some sort of confrontation with her, but I will put it in a nutshell. If I were to describe her as a person and her character, I would have to use the terminology of clinical psychology and perhaps psychiatry. I think I've said enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's move on, then, to Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we know anything now about the influence of Mrs. Plavsic and any control of events, or do we just know that you would need clinical psychology to describe her personality -- which of course, I mean, does not exclude that she had influence or power.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She exerted pressure, as far as I was able to observe, because she wanted to decide on matters that she had neither the talent nor the ability nor the competency to decide upon. There was a big formal problem in this respect. Mrs. Plavsic, together with Mr. Koljevic, had been elected a member of the Presidency in the general election. There was no possibility of anybody budging her from that position unless she resigned. She had no talent whatsoever for any kind of political work. I think the leadership of Republika Srpska understood that, and I don't know whether she agreed to this or not, but they moved her to a position where she would be dealing with humanitarian organisations, women's organisations, and the kind of things that the wives of presidents in large countries do, not members of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me try to keep it short. Are you telling us that beyond that humanitarian area, that Mrs. Plavsic had no influence and did not exercise any power? Is that what you want to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She didn't have influence in the top state leadership, but she sought other channels. She made statements, she toured the country. And we're speaking of 1992 now. Her standpoints were far more radical than mine as regards the methods of the struggle and the results to be expected. But she stated her views in public. I don't believe that could have been seen as the standpoint of the Presidency of the republic, and I think it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me ask a specific question. This Chamber has heard evidence on Mrs. Plavsic saying something about the existence of camps. Would that be something of a -- not something that she said on behalf of the -- on the Presidency or leadership?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that. I cannot be sure when and where she said that, that the camps existed. I would have to know when she said that; however, I'm not able to give you a reliable answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there's any misunderstanding, I didn't intend to ask you -- to tell you that we heard evidence of Mrs. Plavsic saying that camps existed, but about the existence; this could be denying or confirming. But if you are not aware of any such statements, then, Mr. Josse, please proceed. I was a bit too early, Mr. Josse. Judge Hanoteau has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Josse, just a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have spoken to characterise -- or rather, you have said that in her case, this would have been a case for a psychiatrist, there was a clinical situation, but this is not sufficient because in a clinic, of course, there are so many possible cases. So since you are asserting this, could you be a little more precise. What sort of condition would she have had which would have justified her being in a clinic? Could you be precise? Could you be more precise, if you please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, she was a very rigid personality with a very peculiar biography. She was an elderly woman without family or children. She had an artificial attitude towards the new generations. She had a compulsive need to -- a compulsive need for self-affirmation, even when she had no grounds for that, and this always brought her into conflict with her surroundings. The rigidity of her personality and this need for self-affirmation always made her take a dogmatic approach to everything. As we are now speaking of 1992, I think everyone can understand what I mean when I say that she was even more radical than the members of the Serb Radical Party when it came to the methods and the results of the struggle. And five, six, or seven years later she had some personal misunderstandings, not political but personal misunderstandings, with some people from the state leadership, including President Karadzic and his wife, the speaker of the Assembly, and so on and so forth, and this led her to change her political views completely. But she still remained a dogmatic personality. This kind of dogmatic personality structure, well, you can say -- one can say that about everything, and that may be true, but when you have such a mind-set in a plumber or a shoemaker, it doesn't have consequences for all of society. If this is a characteristic of somebody who is in public view every day and who has to make decisions relating to the entire state, the consequences can be dramatic. So you have to view the personality in a certain context. Later on, she denied everything she had done. As for what she was unable to deny, she said she was apologising for it. I cannot quote her words because I haven't seen everything she said, but this was the way she operated, as a dogmatic, inflexible, rigid personality in the state leadership. And President Karadzic, in my view, when candidates were sought for the elections, insisted that she become a candidate because he felt that she would remain -- that she would keep her views, adhere to her previous views, the ones she had had in 1992, that's why he wouldn't hear of another candidate. We had an extensive discussion with the state leadership of Republika Srpska, with Karadzic at its head. I don't know who else was there, but for the most part everybody else kept silent and only President Karadzic spoke. And when I and President Seselj insisted that this would have disastrous consequences, he insisted that she remain a candidate. He was astonished at what she did later on, but I was not because such personality structures, which are always seeking after self-affirmation and, if you insist on my using these terms, they are immeasurably egocentric, everything serves their own personal self-affirmation, even their political work, that's why these conflicts and misunderstandings were bound to arise. From the political aspect, of course this is interpreted quite differently. I am speaking of my own convictions, not of Madeleine Albright's personal convictions. She spoke in different terms than I did. I had observed everything and followed it. Of course this lady made use of all this in view of the policy of the American establishment in order to have Mrs. Plavsic end up where she did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now to Mr. Krajisnik. And firstly, perhaps you could assess his personality and work ethic as you saw it in 1992.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, you're always on slippery ground when you have to answer a question like that. You might insult someone or misinterpret someone's characters, but I will tell you what I feel certain of. I mentioned that before the war I knew Mr. Krajisnik superficially. We'd had a few short encounters. My perception was mostly through the media because he was the president of the National Assembly. During the war I got to know him somewhat better. I met him more than once, and I observed his work more carefully and his standpoints. In any case, he is a highly moral man, of a traditional type of character, a religious type, who is very dedicated to the work he is doing. This is a man who can lay aside all other considerations, including personal and family considerations, in order to carry out the task that has been entrusted to him or a task that he feels to be important. In my evaluation, he is a man who knew other people very well, who knew the mind-set of the various types of people living in Bosnia and Herzegovina, especially in Sarajevo. He was familiar with the Muslim mind-set and way of life. This follows from many years of experience and his need to observe and analyse. He spoke more sparingly than people like me about problems. When I say "people like me," I mean people who do this professionally, speak professionally. I think he had a great respect for the law and legality, and I think that he had a great respect for authority. And I can illustrate this with examples. On one occasion I asked to meet the state leadership to discuss a certain topic. President Karadzic could not receive me and I was received by Mr. Krajisnik. We spoke for about an hour or an hour and a half about pluralism in the republic, the fight against crime, the prospects of the republic, the rule of law and similar topics, about the relationships between the various political parties. And he took copious notes. 24 hours later or some 30 hours later, a meeting was scheduled with Mr. Karadzic, and Mr. Krajisnik repeated the essence of our conversation very correctly. He put forward my suggestions and his reserved response, and then, with great discipline, he waited for Mr. Karadzic, as the president of the republic, to take up a standpoint concerning all this. At that point, Mr. Karadzic's character was displayed. He spoke in very abstract and idealistic terms, like a true psychotherapist, and everything remained as it was. Nothing really changed. I have told you this to show that Krajisnik's attitude to authority was not to do with personalities so much as with the constitution, laws, moral principles, respect for human life regardless of ethnicity or religious affiliation. He was a well-rounded, consistent character, a man with personality, a personality with no gaps or vacancies that can be filled by others, unlike some other people we have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you next assess his skills as a politician.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Krajisnik, as the president of the National Assembly, complied with the constitution. I think he knew where limits or boundaries were. He was very popular before the war for at least two reasons. First of all, because of his persistence and consistency, and also because on every occasion he always showed that he was not the president of only the Serb MPs but of the Assembly as a whole, and there were some who didn't like that. In the situation which arose after April and the arrival in Pale, Mr. Krajisnik found himself in a situation where he had to insist that the National Assembly of Republika Srpska work in compliance with the regulations and not just anyhow. I don't think an Assembly session was ever called that Mr. Krajisnik did not preside over. I never saw that the deputy president of the Assembly ever had an opportunity to chair an Assembly session, although this would have been permitted by the rules. I don't remember Mr. Krajisnik ever participating in any activities that were not strictly prescribed by his term of office. I don't know whether he ever attended cabinet sessions. He may have done, but I don't know of it. There's also something else I can say. As a man of huge energy, he had very many working meetings with representatives of local authorities, Municipal Assemblies, Executive Boards, and various delegations, and these meetings went on forever. So he worked for 15 or 20 hours a day. As far as I know, the topic of those talks - but there are ways that can be established independently - were always something that did not fall outside the competence of his office as president of the Assembly. Other representatives of Republika Srpska authorities were often away on trips, and Mr. Krajisnik was the one who was usually in his office. Whenever I came to Pale and asked who was there, President Krajisnik was always there and nobody else was. Very often you would not be able to find a single minister in the government premises. I didn't say that was always the case, but very often. So people went to see the person who was available, I assume. And if people go to see somebody once and achieve something, even if only a promise, then that prompts them to come to the same person again. They knew that Mr. Krajisnik had the ear of the others and could draw their attention to certain problems or issues or speed things up. They would turn to him. He had huge energy for work, and this is something that caused people to respect his authority. This was a characteristic that had significance in the eyes of others, and it was a by-product of his character.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next issue which follows from that, and to some extent you have just dealt with, is his power in the time that you were in Pale in 1992. How did you or do you assess the power that he had at that time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, would it be a good idea to expand the question to influence and/or power?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So influence and/or power, please, Mr. Poplasen.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Influence and power are two different terms. Power is an abstract, diffuse concept with quite an imprecise meaning, whereas influence means, as I understand it, to what extent Mr. Krajisnik was able to suggest something to others, after which they would do it. I've already said something about this. I think other people opened up to the influence of Mr. Krajisnik on their own rather than him seeking to have influence. His influence stemmed from his character, his personality, and also from his formal post as president of the National Assembly. I don't believe, or at least I didn't notice, that his influence went beyond what was defined in the constitution as the office of the president of the National Assembly. As far as I was able to observe, his working day consisted of numerous meetings and it's hard to say what he discussed and how successfully, but attempting to be an objective observer, those would be my conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were you aware of whether Mr. Krajisnik was a member of an expanded Presidency in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did observe this. This was an invented category. Such a thing does not exist. It's as if you were having lunch and then you ask for a second helping of dessert, and then they describe this as an expanded lunch. An expanded Presidency is not a category that exists in the constitution. The Presidency of the republic, like other state organs in every country, can invite certain people to certain meetings, and then of course, in physical terms, that's expanded; it's a little broader. But had it acted as a kind of expanded Presidency, first of all, it would have been counter-constitutional; secondly, the person convening such sessions not based on law would bear the responsibility. Mr. Krajisnik was not prone to such things, but he was prone to giving his contribution to any situation where he could contribute. I assume he was invited to attend sessions of the Presidency, but if a vote was taken, he would not have the right to vote. I think that's understood. You have put a question to me for which you had a prepared answer: Was he a member of the expanded Presidency? But there was no such thing as the expanded Presidency. According to the law, there was a Presidency, and there was also a possibility of declaring a state of war, and if a state of war was declared, apart from the members of the Presidency, the president of the National Assembly and the Prime Minister would become members of the Presidency, but this would then not be an expanded Presidency but a War Presidency. So I cannot answer your question with a yes or no. If there was an expanded Presidency, then that was contrary to the constitution, and this is something that is completely foreign to my mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I'd rather keep it a bit more factual. Are you aware of meetings of - whether you call it Presidency or not - of meetings of those who would have composed a War Presidency if the conditions for creating a War Presidency would have been met? That is, meetings - not one meeting - regular meetings of Mr. Karadzic, Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. Koljevic, and the speaker of the Assembly, president of the Assembly, and the Prime Minister. Were those meetings held frequently or at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can give you an answer, but not a very decisive one. I know that they did sit together, but whether you can call it a session or a meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, this Chamber has seen minutes of what is called sessions of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina held during imminent threat of war and, just to give you an example, at one of these meetings you were appointed commissioner for Vogosca. We have seen quite a lot of these documents. So my question simply is - let's forget for a second about the constitution and what were the formalities - but whether those five people, who would under the constitution have formed what you call the War Presidency, whether they met at a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. I know this for a fact because I even had deliberate encounters with the Prime Minister because he was a friend of mine from before the war and I knew that he was not present there. I even exerted pressure through him, through the Prime Minister, in order that part of the government might be relocated from Pale to Banja Luka. My belief was that he, as a Prime Minister, could not make sure that the professional services of the government did their role, performed their role outside an urban centre. His answer to this was: I'll see when I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most often he answered by saying: I'll see what I can do about it when I get to see the president. And then some 20 days would pass. So evidently he wasn't present at this session where the state of war was declared. Mr. Krajisnik was physically located --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about one specific. I asked whether these five persons would meet frequently, and I gave you as one example the meeting where you were appointed commissioner for Vogosca. You come with a long story. Are you aware or are you not aware of frequent meetings of these five persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I have given you my answer: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you knew for a fact that they would not frequently meet. What's the basis -- or did I misunderstand you? You said: "I know this for a fact because ..." and then you gave a long non-conclusive reasoning. Could you be certain about -- that they would not frequently meet, apart from conclusions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In answering your question, I mentioned the Prime Minister himself who would have been -- had he been there, I would have known. So I cannot give you any additional detail. So if he wasn't there, there wasn't five of them but four of them. Then I also continued saying that Mr. Krajisnik was located in the same -- located on the same premises. So I was -- I was trying to give you a direct answer, but you cannot ask of me to be certain. I wasn't a member of the Presidency and I wasn't there. I don't know what the possibilities were. They might have even decided to have coffee together and then somebody produced minutes, and this turned out to be a session. I cannot say because I cannot describe events I did not take part in, and that's why I cannot give any conclusive statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you expect Mr. Karadzic to sign such make-up minutes, or was that part of just someone making minutes of coffee meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really can't say. I can only tell you the following: Had they consulted me, I would have the minute-keeper take the minutes first and then I would ask the president of the republic to sign the minutes. That's what I would do. At least, that's how the minutes were kept in my office. I would have insisted on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed -- Mr. Josse, I'm looking at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a question before we break. A while ago, talking about Mr. Krajisnik, you said: [In English] "I think that he had a great respect for the law and legality, and I think that he had a great respect for authority. And I can illustrate these with examples. On one occasion I asked to meet the state leadership to discuss a certain topic. President Karadzic could not receive me and I was received by Mr. Krajisnik." [Interpretation] I would like you to help us to understand this sentence. Does this mean there was a sort of possible activity between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic? You seem to put them on the same footing, while if I understand they had powers, or they were -- I suppose you have very different powers. Mr. Karadzic is absent, so I'm received by Mr. Krajisnik to discuss a matter and I should meet those of the leadership. So what did you actually want to say when you said that? Do you understand my question? I suppose you do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I've understood you well, of course both of them are members of the state -- were members of the state leadership of Republika Srpska; that's why I put them on the same plane. And my party and I recognised the legitimacy of the leadership. Regardless of all the differences of opinion, they were members of the leadership of Republika Srpska. Mr. Krajisnik was the president of the parliament, and it is only understandable that he was in charge of the matters of pluralism, legality, passage of legislation, election matters, and so on and so forth. Mr. Karadzic was not only president of the republic but also president of the SDS, the ruling party, which had absolute power. Besides, this was the party that insisted that we support them on various matters and positions. Sometimes we provided the support, sometimes we did not, as I explained. Therefore, the persons one ought to have spoken to were both of them; however, it is understandable that the Serbian Democratic -- Radical Party -- the Serbian Democratic Party was to formulate its positions through the president. Therefore, my conversation with the vice-president of the SDS had to ultimately be verified by the president. That's why, to cut the procedure short, I went to see the president. When I arrived in Pale, he was busy, he had some obligations to attend to - I don't remember which ones - I went to see Mr. Krajisnik and seized the opportunity to talk to him about the details concerning our views and positions because I knew that I was not going to be given much time to elaborate on these with Mr. Karadzic. It was in this sense that I had stated that. But of course he -- their positions were quite different, and the situation wasn't that they -- whatever one could do, the other could do as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break until 25 minutes to 5.00

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. To keep matters short, of course not giving a final decision on the matter, but it was reported to one of the legal officers of the Chamber, as requested by the court officer, the CLSS has checked the disputed translation of the document referred to below and confirmed the accuracy of the translation done by CLSS. So if you would further like to dispute the matter, then it should be taken at a higher level. At least you would need -- at least you would need to come up with some experts, linguistical experts. I hope you understand this position. I don't know whether there was any further disagreement. I also note that of course it's not the core of the document. I mean, these are nuances and I wonder whether it's worthwhile to ask further expertise for these nuances. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, you've been answering questions about an expanded Presidency. Did Nikola Koljevic ever say anything to you which suggested there was such an institution in being?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember him mentioning these -- this expression of an expanded Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Anyone else?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Apologies. Perhaps an additional remark should be made here because there was a similar question put to me by Their Honours. It was quite logical to me that in view of the fact that the Presidency was passing a number of laws at the time, I was interested in knowing when, in fact, the MPs could meet or could not. It was quite logical, in fact, for the state leadership to have acted the way they have in the circumstances when the parliament could not meet. Now, who came up with the term of an expanded Presidency to simply satisfy this as a formality, I cannot fathom.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to now ask you some specific questions. As far as you were aware, was Mr. Krajisnik able to instruct or tell the government what to do?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you for a fact that not only was he in the -- in the -- that -- it's not that he would -- he was not in a position to do that, and besides, the Prime Minister would not have obeyed anyway because the Prime Minister was quite different from Mr. Krajisnik as a personality and was not really sympathetic with Mr. Krajisnik. I think it would be Mr. Djeric who would object first to anything of the kind done by Mr. Krajisnik and would say that it was anti-constitutional.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: A similar question in relation to the Presidency: Was Mr. Krajisnik able to tell them what to do?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know the persons involved, I suppose that Mr. Karadzic always heard out Mr. Krajisnik, but which of the matters he indeed agreed to and accepted is unknown to me. Knowing Mr. Krajisnik, he on his part must have showed persistence. Now, in which way these two personalities interacted was -- would be in the realm of conjecture; it's difficult to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Krajisnik have the power to punish individuals?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he punished his children on several occasions at Pale because they had violated some of his instructions, but the rest I can only imagine. And I can tell you that he was quite skillful at disciplining his children because they were very well-behaved.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to now turn, if I may, please, to the army. Did Mr. Krajisnik have any power or control over the army, as far as you were aware?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the top civilian leader was the president of the republic, and he was the commander-in-chief. The president of the parliament had nothing to do with the army directly or indirectly. That would constitute a direct violation of the law. Even had he tried to exert this influence, he would have had to informally order the commander to do something, and the commander in question would have had to know that this was against the law. However, based on my knowledge of the man, who I met several times - and I'm talking about General Mladic - I can tell you that from the start he was trying to earn some powers for himself. When Mladic was appointed, it was the first time that I heard of the term "Commander of the Main Staff." Usually the term was the "Chief of the Main Staff." Here there was a chief and a commander of the Main Staff, and from the start I realised that he wanted to secure for himself --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would we agree that the witness has answered your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please, next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The -- I've got three disparate but short topics I would like to deal with in conclusion. The first goes back to the commissioners, one of which you were. I want to ask about the other commissioners and to whom they reported. First of all, are you aware who Mr. Djukanovic reported to?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You probably referring to Mr. Djokanovic, not Djukanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am. My mispronunciation. Thank you for correcting me.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally speaking, all of us were responsible to Mr. Koljevic because he was charged with the task by the Presidency. However, I had known Mr. Djokanovic from before the war, and I knew that he had quite close and even friendly relations with Mr. Karadzic. Perhaps this went along their professions, both of them being physicians. Perhaps I was friends with Mr. Koljevic because both of us dealt with humanities, and I know that very often he contacted Mr. Karadzic. Admittedly, Dr. Djokanovic was not a member of the SDS party, just as I wasn't. He was the president of the Party of the Federalists, as his party was called. But as far as I was able to see, he had regular contacts with Mr. Karadzic, and I suppose that in these contacts they talked about his work on the field and that he sought his advice in that respect. I never came across Dr. Djokanovic and Professor Koljevic sitting together.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I have one moment, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd next like to ask you about another one of your fellow commissioners, Mr. Radovanovic, who I think was in your political party. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Mr. Radovanovic, you see, was in the Serb Democratic Party for a while, up until the outbreak of the war; he was even the spokesperson of the SDS in Sarajevo. I knew him from before the war, and in early April, as he arrived in Pale, he liked me and my ideas much more, and that's why he sided with me. I suppose he found me more appealing than Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: To whom did he report in connection with his work as a commissioner?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Radovanovic was also responsible to Mr. Koljevic, there's no doubt about that, although he was the commissioner of Ilidza municipality. As far as I was able to glean, he was the sort of person who left most of his duties and obligations to the president of the Ilidza Municipal Assembly. In some of our conversations I criticised him for his negligence in work, but I was not his superior in that respect; it was Mr. Koljevic, and he dealt with him. At that time I contacted with Mr. Radovanovic because I sent him out to some of the municipalities because we were setting up boards of the Serbian Radical Party and we had some party-related tasks to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next topic I want to ask you about is a document known in this court as a Variant A and B document. Are you aware of the existence -- were you aware of the existence of that document, either in 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was at a later stage in the recent years and months during the trial against Mr. Krajisnik that I heard about this document and about these Variants A and B. As I was saying yesterday, there were these abstract stories about what the Serb people would do in case of conflict, but there were no differentiating details in terms of 30, 40, 50, or 70 per cent of the Serbian people. I had seen or heard none of that. Had these documents really existed, then they would have probably been strictly party documents of the Serbian Democratic Party. I cannot say that they were -- that they existed or did not because I simply did not hear of them at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: A similar question, Mr. Poplasen, in relation to what is known as the six strategic goals. Was that something that you were made aware of in any guise or form in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to the document itself, then the answer is no; when it comes to its contents, then I can tell you the following: As I was taking a walk with Professor Koljevic around the building at Pale, we would discuss some matters from the history of the people there, and I had this idea on my mind when I was discussing the relations between the Serbian Radical Party and the Serbian Democratic Party. The strict formulation of six strategic goals and their formulation on paper was something I was not aware of, and had I been aware of that, I would have been against that, I would have been opposed to that idea. My version would have been more abstract. This looks like tactics rather than strategy, but the truth is that I did not hear of the document at the time, although I did discuss such matters in one or several of my conversations with Professor Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Poplasen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that concludes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. Harmon, are you ready to cross-examine Mr. Poplasen?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour, I just need to set up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Poplasen, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Harmon, counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would like to begin by clarifying the testimony yesterday about your military service. Yesterday in your testimony you said your military service was as follows: That you joined a unit known as the Nisici Brigade for 20 days, where you helped the commander Slavko Kojic with advice in his command, and then you joined the army only in November of 1994, when you were mobilised into the student brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That evidence, Your Honour, is found at pages 41 and 42 of LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the student brigade, Mr. Poplasen?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether you're referring to the Niksic Brigade or the student brigade. You mentioned both.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm referring to the student brigade.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The student brigade -- well, there are records on that, official military records. I may be wrong by a few days because I haven't got the documents with me, but it might have been about the 15th of November, 1994, I was mobilised, until about the 10th of January, 1995. The dates are approximate. It's in my military booklet, but I cannot really remember it precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What roles and what functions did you have in the student brigade?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the student brigade I was assistant commander of the 1st Battalion for morale and religious issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And who was the commander of the student brigade?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: During these three months, the battalion commanders changed. The first one was Professor Ranko Zrilic; he was a university professor and was not a reserve officer. He was followed by an active-duty officer, whose name was - I hope I'm not wrong about the first name, I'm sure about the last name - I think it was Nenad Radovic. I'm speaking of the 1st Battalion. The brigade commander was somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you to look at an exhibit. If those -- the first volume could be handed to the witness. Mr. Poplasen, these are exhibits you'll see in front of you. They have tab numbers. I will refer you to documents in various tabs, and if you could turn to tab number 2, you will see, Mr. Poplasen, that this is an excerpt from Who's Who in the Republika Srpska. And if we turn to the text under your name, it says as follows, it says: "Dr. Poplasen --"

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I'm referring, Your Honours, to about three-quarters of the way down in the English text.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: "Dr. Poplasen was present at all the front lines, always with a rifle in his hands. He fought shoulder to shoulder with his great friend, legendary Chetnik Major Boro Radic." Do you see that in the text of Who's Who?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this on page 53?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. It should be on page 52 or 53 in the Cyrillic. I -- and it should be in the -- it should be -- Mr. Poplasen, it should be in the Cyrillic text on the right-hand column --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, is there a possibility that page 53 ends approximately, in Cyrillic, where in English it would read: "And in June 1992 he was appointed as war commissioner"? Because I --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It could, Your Honour, yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I see "June of 1992" on the last line of page 53, so therefore I think we would need page 54 to find the relevant passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If there's another bundle, I can give it to Mr. Karganovic to assist. The problem is --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It may well be that this is defective in terms of the copy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From what I read it's -- there's hardly -- the lower part of page 2 does not appear on page 53 --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik is telling me he doesn't think it's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I don't either, Your Honour, so I will pass on this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon is going to find page 54, if he still thinks it important enough to present the witness with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, while I sort out this issue, let me ask you: Did you fight shoulder to shoulder with a Chetnik Major Boro Radic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, the way you put the question is "shoulder to shoulder." Of course the "no" is multi-interpretable. Did you fight together with the person just mentioned, Mr. Boro Radic?
