utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood the Prosecutor. I was not a soldier or a fighter in Vogosca at all, and I participated in no battles at all. Boro Radic was not a major, that was just his nickname. He was a civilian. He was a lad who for a long time had been in the Foreign Legion. He returned home a year or two before the war broke out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. The question is, that's the main issue, whether you ever were involved together with him in any armed operation, wherever, whenever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, I'd like you to turn to tab 39, if you would, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I have not invited for tab 2 to provide a number. Perhaps it was clairvoyance because it was not complete anyhow. But let's just look at 39, whether that would need a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It does, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 2, Your Honour, would be P1074; and tab 39 would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, tab 2 not yet. Tab 2 should be completed first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 39 would be P1074.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if you return to the document in Cyrillic, this is a -- appears to be a copy of a document from the Central Homeland Commission in Belgrade, dated 20 March 1994. It is a document which, at the end, is typed the name "President of the Central Homeland Administration and Council of Vojvodas, Vojvoda Dr. Vojislav Seselj." And if you turned in this document to, in the B/C/S version in front of you, to the second page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 190 in the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: 190 in the original, and in the English it's page 2 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You'll see your name is mentioned, and your name is mentioned as being a vojvoda. First of all, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is, to the best of my recollection, a copy of the original document and it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the text in the document, Mr. Poplasen, it reads -- and I'm going to read a sentence. It says: "He actively participated and commanded the Niksic Brigade from May 1992 to June of 1992 and then he moved to the intervention unit of the Vogosca Brigade." I want you to focus your attention on the latter part of the sentence. Did you, in fact, move to the intervention unit of the Vogosca Brigade? Did you participate in that brigade, in that unit?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did you ever assume command of the Niksic Brigade?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, never. I was not among the commanders anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Poplasen, if we could turn next to a document that is found at tab 59, and if you would -- first of all, Mr. Poplasen, there is a -- in the B/C/S version, the first page -- first page of that document should have a cover. It's from a book. If you take a look at that, it bears the likeness of Mr. Seselj. It should be at the first page of B/C/S in that, tab 59.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When we are still searching, we can invite the registrar to assign a number to tab 59.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 59, Your Honours, would be P1079 -- 75.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It may well be -- it may well be missing from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, it's been found; I can see it from here, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: First of all, this cover, which bears the ERN number 03461266 in the right-hand side of the upper part of the page, bears a picture of Mr. Seselj, does it not?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this book that was published by Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I have to look at it, and that might jog my memory. He's published over a hundred books, so I can't remember every single title.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, let me take you to a part of the book, if I can, Mr. Poplasen. If you could turn to page 183 of the Cyrillic text --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry to be pedantic, Your Honour: Can we know what the book is called?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we have a problem as well. Mr. Harmon, tab 59 I received only the first five pages out of 25, but I see that my colleague Judge Hanoteau is in the possession, and Judge Canivell as well, in possession of the front page of the book. I am punished, says Judge Hanoteau.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If you are missing it, Your Honour, I will make sure that you receive a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And do we have the title of the book, as Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It does not appear in my English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So perhaps you can assist us, Mr. Poplasen. Can you read into the record the title of this book. You'll find that again with a picture of Mr. Poplasen -- with a picture of ...

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if you can hear me. The author is Dr. Vojislav Seselj. "In Sinisa Aksentijevic's Focus." Then it says "Serb Radical Party," that's evidently the publisher. The title is "The Philippics of the Chetnik Vojvoda."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much for assisting us. Mr. Poplasen, what I want to direct your attention to is, first off, if you turn to page 183 of the Cyrillic text --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if I can direct Your Honours to page 3 of 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Have you found 183, Mr. Poplasen?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 183, I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, this identifies the commanders and it gives a series of ranks. You'll see that, starting with subpart A, lance corporals, and it goes through a series of ranks, ending with subpart I, which says: "Vojvodas, commanders of bigger units, compositions, or regions." A few minutes ago, Mr. Poplasen, you told us that you were a vojvoda. Tell us, if you will, what military responsibilities you had as a vojvoda.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no military responsibilities. I was not a military person at all, not a soldier, except for the period I've already mentioned when I was in the student brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Then can you explain to the Trial Chamber what the title meant in respect of you if it did not have military connotations.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I can explain that, but it might be more interesting to ask why you're showing this at all to Their Honours. This is a historical representation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, it's not up to you to ask the Prosecution why he puts a certain question to you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the historical tradition, the Chetnik movement had a certain structure which was not as precise as the one represented here by Mr. Seselj. The rank of vojvoda was awarded within the Chetnik movement even to village headmen. These were not large-scale military formations, and this was actually an honourary title. The life of the Serbs in the 18th, 19th, and 20th century was characterised by fighting, from the fighting in Macedonia before World War I onwards. Another point is there were no Chetnik units in the Army of Republika Srpska at all. First of all, they were banned, they were prohibited by the regulations of Republika Srpska; secondly, the Serb Radical Party abolished the Chetnik movement as an independent formation in its constitution; and thirdly, at the outset in June/July, when the war broke out, I made several public speeches --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, let me interrupt you for just a minute. My question was: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber what the title of vojvoda meant in respect of you. Was it an honourary title? Was it bestowed upon you for any particular service in the Serb radical movement? Can you enlighten us as to why you had the title vojvoda.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm proud of my title. It is an expression of respect, of paying tribute to certain moral qualities. It has no other connotations or content.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And why was it bestowed upon you, Mr. Poplasen?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was bestowed on me because I was constantly present in Republika Srpska from the very beginning of the war, because I advocated the unification of the Serbian people and the traditional values of the Serbian people living in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if we turn to the photograph that is at the front, found in tab 1, Mr. Poplasen, I have some questions to ask you about that particular photograph. Can you tell us when that photograph was taken and where it was taken?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This photograph was taken -- well, I can't remember the exact date, but it would have to be in the summer of 1992, some hundred or so metres away from Hotel Panorama at Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you assign a number to that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 1 would be P1076, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And was this the type of a uniform that was issued by the VRS or was this a typical Chetnik uniform?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a uniform at all, either one or the other; it's traditional national dress, Serbian traditional folk costume. This is the kind of clothing that the Serbs wore in traditional times, up until World War II. They wore it as their Sunday best, when they went to church, to fairs, to weddings, and other ceremonial occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Poplasen. Let me focus, if I can, on your views of representatives of the international community. If we could turn, first of all, to tab 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could have an exhibit number for tab 7.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 7 would be P1077, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, this does not have a B/C/S translation, Mr. Poplasen. Do you read English?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would need the assistance of an interpreter. I have the text before me, but I would like some assistance from the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, I will assist you, Mr. Poplasen. In August of 1993, as chairman of the Serb Radical Party in the Republika Srpska, you publicly supported retaliation against UNPROFOR members if air strikes were to take place in the Republika Srpska. Isn't that correct? In this text from Tanjug reads -- I'll read the first sentence: "Nikola Poplasen, chairman of the Serb Radical Party, SRS, in the Republika Srpska said in Banja Luka today that if air strikes against Serb positions were carried out, the SRS would call for retaliation against UN Protection Forces, UNPROFOR members." Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the term "retaliation" is the appropriate word to use. I'm not sure that "retaliation" is the right word because it implies some kind of physical activity. I was probably thinking of non-obedience, expulsion, something like that, however, we couldn't expel them because we were too weak for that. In my assessment we did not have the strength to enter into a conflict with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how this term has been translated here, whether the journalist used the right word. "Retaliation," does that mean resistance? It could be resistance. In any case, my position was what I have just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, let me give you another term. This is found in tab 6 of the binder before you. This is a document -- a publication, it's from Serb Glas Srpski. I will read this to you. You're familiar with the journal Glas Srpski, Mr. Poplasen?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. This is a daily paper published in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would have number 10 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1078, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- 78. Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is an article dated the 19th of August, 1993, entitled -- and the subject says: "Serbian Radical Party threatens to kill UNPROFOR members." I'll read the text. "Banja Luka, 18 August. 'If any part of Republika Srpska is bombed, the Serbian Radical Party will call on all its sympathisers in the Serbian people to physically liquidate members of UNPROFOR and all the members of Croatian nationality and Muslim faith who have not taken up arms to fight for the borders and sovereignty of Republika Srpska, even though they live in its territory.' This was said, among other things, at a press conference of the SRS in Banja Luka. Nikola Poplasen, president of the SRS, also talked about the option on the opinion of the Serb Radicals as regards the current process of the Geneva negotiations." So I put to you, Mr. Poplasen, that if the term "retaliation" is not the correct term, did you, in fact, say at this particular press conference that you would call upon the members of the Radical Party and its sympathisers to liquidate members of UNPROFOR and all members of Croatian nationality and Muslim faith who have not taken up arms to fight for the borders and sovereignty of Republika Srpska? Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. This can only be a forgery. I don't know what sort of mind could invite one people to liquidate the other. That's extreme -- that's an extreme position. As far as UNPROFOR members are concerned, I've explained to you a moment ago: From the very start, my position was that they should not be allowed entry in Bosnia and Herzegovina; however, as they were stronger than we were and did not ask for our permission, they were there. Perhaps someone else uttered these harsh formulations, and -- although I suppose there was some sort of propaganda behind these words in motivating them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention, Mr. Poplasen, to 1995 when the United Nations Protection Force members were taken hostage and, among other things, handcuffed to the top of radio transmitters near Jahorina and other locations in Bosnia and within the Republika Srpska. Do you remember those events?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention then to tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if I could get a number for tab 3.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be P1079.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is in English, so I will read this to you, Mr. Poplasen. This is dated the 30th of May. It is attributed to SRNA, and it reads in the top paragraph: "Nikola Poplasen, deputy chairman of the Serb Radical Party of the Serb lands (SRS) today voiced full support for the Bosnian Serb army, BSA, in connection with the capture of UNPROFOR members who have openly sided with the NATO and UN terrorist actions. The SRS leader for Bosnian Serb Republic told a news conference in Banja Luka that the SRS recently advocated that the UNPROFOR forces be declared occupying forces and that the BSA treat them as an army of occupation." First off, did you say that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall this at this time. This was the 30th of May, 1995, but I can't say that the position expressed is not similar to mine; it is. But how can I remember what happened on the 30th of May, 1995, when I made statements every day?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So if you can't remember specifically this statement, Mr. Poplasen, this certainly represented the position that you took at the time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me turn to -- next turn to tab 8 in the materials before you, Mr. Poplasen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 8 would be P1080.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And there are two tabs, I'm told, in this exhibit; there's 8A and 8B for Your Honours' and Mr. Poplasen's edification.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is, first of all, Mr. Poplasen, 8A, as you will see in the Bosnian version. Turn to -- is -- 8A, Bosnian version, you will see this is an interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Perhaps if Mr. Poplasen could have some assistance from the usher in this regard. It's a little bit confusing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: But what I'd like to direct your attention, first of all, Mr. Poplasen, is to 8A, which is an interview that is found in a newspaper. That newspaper Nezavisne Novine in Banja Luka, interview attributed to February the 2nd, 2000. First of all, do you remember giving that interview, Mr. Poplasen?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember talking to Radmilo Sipovac, and I gave several interviews to this paper. There's no reason for me to doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. What I'd like to do, Mr. Poplasen, this reports in the interview -- I'll direct your attention to the upper left-hand corner, there's a number 6. If you turn the cover page you'll see in the upper left-hand corner the number 6. What I'd like to ask you about, Mr. Poplasen, is: In your capacity as the president of the Republika Srpska, you presented medals to Mr. Karadzic, General Mladic, Mr. Martic, General Galic, and Mr. Seselj, all of whom were indicted by this institution. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, to the ones you mentioned now, but not to all of those who were indicted by this institution. But the ones you mentioned here now, yes, that's right, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you were asked the following questions, and I'll read from the text, Mr. Poplasen. The text I'm reading from, for your benefit, is the far left-hand column of the B/C/S version in front of you on page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is on page 2 of 19 in the English version, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Starting at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: "On the Republika Srpska national day in the capacity of RS president, you presented medals to Karadzic, Martic, Mladic, Galic, and Seselj. Were the medals delivered to them?" Your answer: "The process of making the medals is a rather lengthy one and the decision was made immediately prior to the Republika Srpska national day. The medals are such that they can be made only by a small number of people since the technology of production is extremely complex." Then the interviewer asks you: "Do you know where you will deliver the medals to them, and will this be done publicly?" Your answer: "I will hand them the medals personally and I will do it on the Republika Srpska." Interviewer: "To all of them? "Poplasen: To all who have been awarded medals. "NN: Among those who were awarded medals is General Galic who is located in The Hague. "Poplasen: I hope that General Galic will not be in The Hague forever and The Hague farce will come to an end and that General Galic, like a number of Serbs who are not as lucky, will return healthy to Republika Srpska." Were those your words in 2000, Mr. Poplasen?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's all very well, Mr. Prosecutor, what you've mentioned now; however, you state that you -- this is -- the year is 2000 and not the year 1992, if you agree with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For some, at the time, I was president of the republic, for others I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, will you please answer the question, whether these were your words in 2000.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they were, in 2 -- in the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, if I direct Your Honours' attention to tab 8B, this is the identical interview that is reproduced from what I -- a site known as the Serbian Unity Congress.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That has no number yet. Would that be 1081, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And it's the identical interview. I just direct Your Honours' attention to the fact that it was re-published.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if I can direct your attention, Witness, to tab 4 of the materials before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that would be number --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1082, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, this is the -- this is in English, Mr. Poplasen. I'm sure you're familiar with its contents. It is the decision removing Mr. Nikola Poplasen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, before you continue, we've now seen a lot of English documents and I'm concerned about Mr. Krajisnik not being able to follow them. Although you read out specific portions, Mr. Krajisnik is not in a position to put that into context. When could we expect translations?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We will get them as soon as possible. Your Honour is aware that we are working under conditions where witnesses change and we had to work with alacrity, so we have not all the translations for these materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Josse, I take it you will have some understanding for the problems the Prosecution is facing, not getting lists of exhibits, et cetera, well in advance. Would there be a possibility for you to see whether any contextual problems would arise in relation to what Mr. Krajisnik could say about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I will, Your Honour. I do understand the problems, and I -- and I'm sure Mr. Krajisnik also appreciates your concern. Could I add one thing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My concern is also the witness. It's a severe disadvantage when important statements, assertions, that he is alleged to have made are put to someone, they can't see it in front of them. Can I urge Mr. Harmon to go extremely slowly when he's putting these sort of matters to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would be glad to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, the document in tab 4, which is entitled "Decision removing Mr. Nikola Poplasen from the office of president of Republika Srpska" is dated the 5th of March, 1999, and this is the decision of the High Representative in removing you from your position as president of the Republika Srpska. That -- and since you can't read English, let me just read parts of it and I will ask you, Mr. Poplasen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you could first ask the witness -- Mr. Poplasen, did you ever receive a B/C/S version of this decision? Were you able to read that, the decision by which you were removed from office? Just so --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. I received it on the 5th of March, both versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then at least we understand that the witness is familiar with the document. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm referring to the English text, Your Honour, on the second page of this document, under "Reasons for removal."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Poplasen, I'm going to read this to you. It says, and I'll read part of it: "President Nikola Poplasen has abused his power, blocked the will of the people of Republika Srpska by hindering the implementation of the election results, refusing to abide by the decisions of the National Assembly, and consistently acting to impede the formation of a legitimate government with the support of the National Assembly, obstructed the implementation of the general framework agreement for peace, acted to trigger instability in Republika Srpska, and thus put peace into risk in the Republika Srpska and in the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina by the following actions ..." and then it lists a series of actions. Those were the reasons that were included in your dismissal. Do you agree with that -- or you may not disagree [sic] with the actions of the High Commissioner, do you agree that those are the reasons he set forth?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I really don't understand your question. Are you asking me whether this is what the text says or whether you're asking for my opinion about the contents?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, I'm not asking for your opinion.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answers I can give are different.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm not asking for your opinion of the text. I accept fully that you do not agree and did not agree at the time with the High Representative's assessment. But do you agree that in the written decision that you have had an opportunity to review in your language, that the reasons that I read to you set out accurately what the High Representative said were the reasons for your removal?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again your question is ambiguous. I do not agree with the reasons stated here. They are presented here accurately, that's true, but I do not agree with the reasons in term of -- in terms of their essence. And then if I can answer to your question in a couple of sentences, I will. Because what is written here is a falsification of reality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You have answered Mr. Harmon's question. I do understand that you'd like to further clarify, and I would say that we'll give you an opportunity, even if Mr. Harmon would not ask you, we would give you an opportunity at a later stage to briefly, not very lengthy, but briefly tell us what your objections were and then rather in terms, not abstract terms, as a falsification of reality because that could be anything. And perhaps Mr. Josse will deal with the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Could I make this observation: I assume that Mr. Harmon is going to ask it, because otherwise what is the point in putting the document in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The point is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The point is -- I take it -- that's at least how I understand it, that Mr. Harmon wants to shed a negative light on the credibility and perhaps reliability of this witness in view of the reasons for which, in the eyes of the High Representative, had to be removed from office.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If -- of course I understand that, but if that's right, this is not a proper way to cross-examine, in my submission. He might as well just submit the document to the Court and the Court can read it. There's no point saying to the witness: Did you receive this from the High Representative, and then not ask the witness whether he accepted it. That is not proper cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I think I was clear enough to Mr. Harmon when I said if he doesn't ask for it, we would give an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honour, I also introduced the document because yesterday the witness touched upon this and said he had been removed, and this is the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do not think Mr. Josse disputes your right to touch upon the subject in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Poplasen, if we can turn back to tab 8 of the document -- of the bundle before you. This is the interview that we saw a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'd like to direct Your Honours' attention to page 3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, if I could direct your attention to the -- again, the B/C/S version, page 6, the second column. You then in this interview comment on the actions of the High Representative, and let me read to you, Mr. Poplasen, your remarks, that are again found in the B/C/S version the second column. Poplasen: "Well, we also declared --" I'm sorry. Let me go to the question above it. "Have you forgotten that the High Representative declared Seselj to be an undesirable person in BH and RS?" Poplasen: "Well, we also declared the High Representative and all of his colleagues to be undesirable persons a long time ago. We never invited them here. They came with tanks and with airplanes as part of a plan according to which Serbdom, the Serbs, and the Serb countries are all supposed to vanish. But nothing is permanent. The presence of the occupiers is of a temporary character." My question, first, Mr. Poplasen: Are those your words?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you assert that there's a plan by the High Representative to make the Serbs, among other things, disappear -- to vanish.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that I said that the High Representative was one of them. He was just one of the small fish involved in the process. I had in mind somebody who was higher up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who did you have in mind higher up that had the plan that would -- in which the Serbdom, Serbs, and the Serb countries are all supposed to vanish? Who did you have in mind when you said that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had in mind the large empires that were so powerful that they were able to form the Fourth Reich.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. And the large empires who would form the Fourth Reich, what countries were in that -- in that category?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, it depends on how much time you can give me to answer the question, because this question cannot be answered with a yes or no --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I didn't ask you for a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I can answer in five sentences only.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I asked you for the identity of the countries that were involved in that group of countries that formed the Fourth Reich.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will refer you to a source which deals with these matters in detail, and then I will answer your question in three sentences only, if you agree. The former advisor to Prime Minister Major, whose name is Ronald Atkinson, wrote two books. One is called "The European Vicious Circle," and the other "The New Dictatorship of Europe." He analytically outlines all the elements which, in my opinion, show convincingly that the European Community has -- bears all the hallmarks of the Fourth Reich, that it is a para-fascist creation, created against the will of the peoples, Germans, Britons, French, and so on, which can be established through opinion polls and different analyses, and that we were experiencing an imperialistic progression from the area, which was in turn provoking ethnic nationalisms, and that's the typical cause-consequence situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you to identify the countries, finally, that consist of the Fourth Reich that you have asserted were part of a plan to make Serbdom, the Serbs, and Serb countries vanish. What are the countries involved in that group of countries?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm answering your question and you're putting it to me again. I told you clearly the European Community --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, you specifically mentioned that against the will of the peoples, Germans, Britons, French. Would you say that Germany, Great Britain, and France were the countries, perhaps among others, who were forming this Fourth Reich?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Establishment. [Interpretation] Political and economic establishment or the leadership of these countries created the organs of the European Community against the political will and conviction of most of the population of, I can repeat, France, Germany, and Great Britain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any countries outside the European Union?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, this is already the realm of an analysis. There are always those who wish to fulfil their own interests and side with someone, like in World War II. It wasn't easy to find partners in the Albanian or Muslim establishments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just asking whether you had any specific countries in mind outside the EU.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you mention them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already mentioned the Albanian establishment that is trying to come closer to the German interests. For instance, the Muslim world is facing the same dilemma that they had been facing in World War II, whether to cooperate with these establishments or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, I'm just asking for any specific countries, not in a lengthy explanation on them. So you called the Albanians. Any other country you would have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. I was drawing the following distinction: When I said "Germany," I did not mean the German people. I said the establishment. And when I said "France," I didn't mean the French people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean political leadership or any establishment of any other country you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the Balkans are concerned, I mentioned the Albanians and the Albanian leadership in Kosovo. As far as Bosnia-Herzegovina is concerned, I mentioned the Muslim leadership. As far as Croatia is concerned, from the beginning it had been forging a plan with Germany to break up Yugoslavia, and that's the Croatian leadership. As far as Slovenia is concerned, the situation there is clear, too. Within this trend, there was the resistance in the Serbian --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, we've now had Croatia, we've had Slovenia, we had Albanians, Albanian leadership in Kosovo. Any other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that's enough for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Aside, Mr. Poplasen, those countries that you assert to have a plan to make the Serbs in Serb countries and Serbdom vanish, you publicly also stated, isn't it the case, that the Tribunal was created, in part, to assist in that effort?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I would agree with you that this Tribunal is a political institution and that it has certain political tasks to perform, but do you think I'm naive enough to think that this Tribunal or the Judges are supposed to go and commit genocide over the Serbian people? No, that's too far-fetched, too naive. The Hague Tribunal is an institution within the imperial spreading of the European Community -- or rather, the reinstated Fourth Reich. But you keep mentioning a plan as if there was a plan. It's rather a historical process.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, let's take a look and see what you did say about the Tribunal, Mr. Poplasen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We will be playing a video, Your Honour. If I could have an exhibit number for the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We find that under --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Transcript under tab --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is Extra 1, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Extra 1, yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be P1083, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be for the one dated 10 August 1996?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, that is the one 10 August 1996. This is an interview with SRT.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We'll play it. Mr. Poplasen, if you could look at the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "A viewer from Banja Luka is asking Mr. Poplasen what the representatives of the Radicals think about The Hague Tribunal and if Alija Izetbegovic will ever be indicted by that institution? "Well, Alija and The Hague Tribunal belong to one ... It's a political institution and the purpose of its creation is a pogrom of the Serbian people."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You said that, Mr. Poplasen, in August of 1996, did you not?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if we turn to tab 9, Mr. Poplasen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, may I take it that it's part of your questions if the witness would briefly want to comment, he has an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, Mr. Poplasen, if you'd like to briefly comment on your own words or explain so that the Chamber better understands your words, you have an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course I don't object to that, but could I say I have no problem when Mr. Harmon doesn't do that in relation to the words uttered previously by the witness. That is proper in cross-examination, in my submission. The distinction I draw is in relation to statements or assertions by a third party being related to him which he can't comment upon. Can I make that clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that, but at the same time if, for example, it reads "it is a political institution," that is a very short phrase with which people might mean different things, like it was created by politicians, it was the -- the Judges are --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. I'm happy for him to comment. I'm just saying I'm not insisting, if I can put it like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, Mr. Poplasen, not lengthy statements, but if you would like to clarify any of these matters, not the full political context, but especially there where there might be a risk of misunderstanding, you're invited to do so. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was during a pre-election campaign, August 1996, the first elections were soon to take place in the republic, and of course in a television interview where there was more than one participant, as you were able to see, one has to speak briefly and concisely, using expressions that most voters will understand. It's true that I said this, but when I said "pogrom" I wasn't referring to killing, actual killing, taking lives. I was speaking historically, as the Prosecutor said. Modern Western politicians call this de-nationalisation, the loss of all ethnic and national elements. If Serbs no longer speak the Serbs' language, keep Serb traditions, have a Serb culture, that's what this means. I'm speaking about a historical process. Maybe this will happen; it's happened to many peoples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So should we understand this, that where you use the word "pogrom" that it was very short for an attack on the Serbian people's identity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Among other things, yes. Identity, conditions of life, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we can turn next, Mr. Poplasen, to tab number 9. Again, Mr. Poplasen, I will have to read this to you and I'm going to ask you if these are your words. This --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: First of all, if I could have an exhibit number for tab number 9.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be P1084, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: P1084, Mr. Poplasen, is a -- from the United Nations liaison office from Belgrade. It's dated the 8th of January, 1998. The description is: "Poplasen: ICTY is an instrument of American domination." And the summary says, I'll read part of it: "The leader of Vojislav Seselj's Serbian Radical Party in Bosnia, the SRS, Nikola Poplasen, gave an interview to the Belgrade daily Demokratija where he was quoted as saying that the ICTY was an instrument of American domination and directly opposed to international law." Do you remember making that statement or similar statements?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I don't recall this but it closely resembles my standpoints. I would not deny this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And when you say that the ICTY is "directly opposed to international law," what did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt, Your Honour. Where does that take us?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I think it goes to, among other things, the witness's attitude toward this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Harmon, of course we've seen now a few examples. Is there any need to go in further details and ask for an explanation in legal terms? It seems as if Mr. Poplasen is not a great supporter of this institution and that he, in his political life, uses strong language to express that view, and that it's not only that he's not happy with it politically but that he even challenges -- that's at least what my first impression is, that he challenges the legality of this institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I was giving him in the opportunity, as I thought the Court wanted, to briefly comment on certain parts of the statements that I am presenting to this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can withdraw the question and am happy to move on to the next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I summarised in this way and I take it that the parties would agree that this is the first impression of -- of what the witness has told us in this respect, apart from other parts of his testimony, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, I have no objection, as such, to the witness answering the question. This cross-examination is gratuitous, in our submission, and is conducted for a gratuitous and unfair purpose, but I, as such, have no objection to the witness answering the question. He clearly can handle himself quite well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time Mr. Josse asked you a question, the Chamber adds to it, not in where it leads us but what it would add to what we heard of course on this specific subject already.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have one more example, Your Honour, I would like to bring to the Court's attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, if that's the last one, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. It's already an exhibit, Your Honour. It's found at tab 8. It is Exhibit P1080.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, if you could turn back to your interview that's found in tab 8. I want to direct your attention to some comments that are found in that interview, Mr. Poplasen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I direct Your Honours' attention to page 18 of 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, I direct your attention to page 6, again the box that is found, small box, small rectangle on page 6 of the top, "Hag - Instrument Sile." Let me read this into the record. NN -- NN refers to the interviewer: "Do you personally acknowledge the authority of The Hague Tribunal? "Poplasen: I do not acknowledge it personally, on behalf of my party or on behalf of my nation. How can I acknowledge an institution which is contrary to all elementary norms, principles of humanity, legality and justice, which represents a political institution and is the instrument of the policies of hegemonistic, huge totalitarian fascist power? "NN: Apparently you have a higher regard for The Hague inmates than for the Hague court. "Poplasen: They are my friends. The majority of them are acquaintances. Some are colleagues. How could I not hold them in high regard? It is pointless for me to identify with the executioners and spit on the victims." Mr. Poplasen, are those your words? Were you were making that statement?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. When you referred to "the victims," are you saying that the people who had been indicted and who have been arrested and have been brought to this institution for trial are victims? Is that your meaning?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some, yes, not all. But some people who are arrested and brought to The Hague Detention Unit are victims and they are completely innocent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That concludes this area of examination, Your Honour. I don't know what time we're going to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are. As a matter of fact, we're already very late. I would like to add one question, Mr. Poplasen, since you have, it seems, a specific opinion about some of the detainees to be victims and others not. Do you have any specific opinion about the accused in this case, Mr. Krajisnik, to what category he belongs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to what I know, he has not committed any crimes; therefore, he is a victim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We'll have a break for 20 minutes. We'll restart at 25 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a short matter perhaps I could deal with immediately after the break for a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, you asked for one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps it's something I should know but I'm afraid I don't. I reserve my position as to the admissibility of these exhibits, and it's a matter, no doubt, in the usual way, the Chamber will consider when the witness is finished. I'm concerned about those documents where a small part had been referred to. Can I ask: Does the Chamber read the rest of the documents? In other words, if a small part is put into evidence, as opposed to admitted into evidence, does the Chamber read the whole document? And if the document is then admitted as an exhibit, does the position change? I obviously need to know that to decide what I need to re-examine upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, I -- you may have noticed that the Chamber often tries to reduce the size of the documents so as to have the immediate context and not anything else. If from several portions of a document quotes are put to a witness, then we usually read the whole of the document. So if there would be anything else in that document that would require cross-examination, then we would then read that. So we try to resolve the matter by reducing the size of what is presented in evidence, but if it's there, we can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course we'll mainly focus on -- we'll mainly focus on the portions addressed by the parties, and we'll not a start an in-depth search to see whether there's anything else we could find. But if our eye -- we will read it --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So can I just be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I may object to its admissibility, but leaving that aside P1075, the extract from Mr. Seselj's book, one line has been put to the witness and the rest of it may be read by the Chamber and used as evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that about Mr. Poplasen -- about Mr. Krajisnik or --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I presume not. I haven't had a chance to read it, but one of the things I need to know is whether I really do need to read it tonight to be in a position to re-examine the witness upon it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, is there any way you would reduce the size of the portion of the book and limit the evidence to the relevant portions and the direct context on the page? Usually we say one page before and one page after that so that we can place the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And can you inform Mr. Josse what parts you will take out so he doesn't have to do any unnecessary reading tonight.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will be glad to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have a few other matters. Madam Usher, perhaps you can -- I have to read for some six to seven minutes a few decisions, and perhaps you could already take care that the witness is stand-by and nearby. I first would like to give a statement on behalf of this Chamber on decisions of Bosnian courts. The Trial Chamber would like to address the parties regarding the presentation of material in the form of decisions from Bosnian courts dealing with the prosecutions of crimes in Bosanski Novi municipality during the indictment period. During the testimony on the 15th of December of Witness Pasic, and I refer to transcript page 19700, the Chamber asked the parties to verify the existence of this material and to consider submitting it into evidence. On the 23rd of February, I refer to transcript page 20838, the Defence opposed the introduction of this evidence. The Defence objected on the "identical" grounds that they objected to recently -- to the recently requested evidence regarding Husein Hotic, namely that Rule 98 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence must be interpreted in light of Rule 85. The Defence's submission is that the latter rule places timing constraints on the Chamber's powers under the former rule. We do not agree with the Defence's interpretation. The Chamber may depart from the sequence laid down by Rule 85 where the interests of justice allow. The Chamber remains interested in receiving material relevant to the testimony of Witness Pasic or that may shed light on potentially relevant circumstances within Bosanski Novi. It is in the interests of justice that this evidence be received at the earliest date possible. The Chamber, therefore, directs the parties to agree on the type and amount of material to be submitted by the 23rd of March. In the event that they are unable to agree, the Chamber requests written or oral submissions from both parties regarding their position on the material, again by the 23rd of March. This concludes the matter of the -- on the legal decisions of the Bosnian courts. The next issue is admission of recently translated exhibits. The Trial Chamber would like to address the issue of admitting recently translated exhibits tendered by both parties. These exhibits were submitted during the testimony of previous witnesses and are now available for entry into the trial record. For the Prosecution, that would be P970 and P1073 that have been translated. For the Defence, it would be D106, D113, and D141 that also have been translated. The Chamber will instruct the registry to admit these documents into evidence unless the parties raise objections before the close of business on the 13th of March. Additionally, on the 8th of March the Defence expressed its intention to tender into evidence the video footage provided to them by the Prosecution regarding a Muslim attack on a JNA convoy in Tuzla on the 15th of May, 1992. I would ask, if the Defence is now in a position to offer it for admittance, that the registrar assign the footage an exhibit number and admit it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That was Mr. Stewart's position yesterday, and it's one I echo today, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the Chamber asks that the Defence then accomplishes this by the 14th of March. I think Mr. Stewart said that he would like to have it admitted into evidence, or am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What are you asking the Defence to accomplish? Sorry, I don't follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, no, I think we asked him whether he wanted to tender that material.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the answer was yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question now is if it's there, to be assigned a number; if not, then you're invited to accomplish --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, the registrar physically needs the material. I'm sorry, I'm being slow on the uptake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, without the physical material, we might have a problem. So by the 14th of March this material is expected. That concludes, then, the matter of exhibit admission. Finally I'd like to deal with a list of criminal cases before the courts of Kotor Varos regarding prosecutions of crimes committed against the civilian population during the indictment period. The Chamber would like to address the Defence regarding this list. The Chamber, under Rule 98, has sought access to material on other occasions to assist in the understanding and evaluation of the evidence presented. It has done so in respect of both Prosecution and Defence witnesses. Witness D14 testified on the 23rd of January, 2006, and I refer to transcript page 20257, that he was aware of the existence of a list of 30 cases showing that crimes committed against the civilian population during the indictment period were prosecuted by courts of Kotor Varos. The Chamber asked the witness whether he would be able to provide this list to the Court. The witness readily replied that he would try to do so and, in addition, at transcript page 20260, Witness D14 testified that he believed that such a list had been provided to him by Defence counsel here in The Hague. The Chamber is interested to learn about active prosecutions against those who allegedly committed crimes against the civilian population during the indictment period. The Chamber would like to inquire of the Defence if it has such a list; and, if so, to provide it to the Court by Monday, the 13th of March. If the Defence does not possess this document, the Chamber asks the Defence to take measures to obtain it from Witness D14 and provide it to the Court no later than Friday, the 24th of March. This concludes this issue. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Two things briefly, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I turned it on. Two things, Your Honour: The first item you have requested, decisions of the Bosnian courts, you referred to various pages in the transcript. The state of play is this: Within a day or two of the Court making that request, I provided to the Defence a list of exhibits of documents from the case file that is referred to, and it's -- at this point it's under consideration by the Defence, as far as I know. So we have identified the documents and we are awaiting a reply from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, I said that the Chamber therefore directs the parties to agree on the type and the amount to be submitted, and if they're unable to agree, that the Chamber then requests written and oral submissions -- or oral submissions on the matter. So we did understand that the Defence is now in possession of that material and that -- well, of course, in order to agree upon something, Mr. Josse, Mr. Harmon expects a position taken by the Defence, but that goes without saying, I would say. The Chamber just waits whether you could agree upon it; if not, then we'll hear further submissions and we might order either the whole bunch of it or whatever or nothing at all. That's -- is that clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's clear, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The second item is that we have the missing page from the document that was found in tab 2. Those have been distributed, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And it now needs an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you are going to put that to the witness again, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm not sure I need to. I read to him and I put the proposition to him as set forth in tab 2, and he said that didn't happen. So I'm happy to put it to him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then wait whether you use that now complete document in your further evidence, and then we would assign a number to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yeah, I don't intend to use it further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's something I will be objecting to. Whether the Court wants to assign a number to it now and listen to my objections at the end of the witness's evidence, or whether the Court would like to hear my submissions now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It will take 30 seconds. The submission is: The witness totally denied it; it therefore has no value whatsoever. It comes from a book, an extract of a book, the witness totally denies; it can be ignored by this Chamber, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which then means that there is no need to use the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure that the mere denial is sufficient. I think the Court can consider it when it considers other sources of material as to this witness's military service. He's stated a proposition. He was in the Nisici Brigade and he was in the students brigade, and that was it. And I put to him a number of sources that go to his credibility. I think it should be assigned a number. What weight the Court gives it ultimately is up to the Trial Chamber but I think it merits a number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whether we need a document for that -- Mr. Josse, I take it that you do not deny the existence of the document from which Mr. Harmon read?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely. I'm not suggesting the Prosecution have forged it in any way whatsoever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the question then remains whether we use that document in the evidence to evaluate the testimony of this witness, where it seems not to be in dispute among the parties where someone has written this in some book.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that whether we need the document to further then assess credibility and reliability, of course it's a matter always of evaluating the totality of the evidence. If someone would -- I could tell you there are some books which write things about me which are not true. At the same time, there are not hundreds of them. So therefore, it's -- comes to context, it comes to -- but it's also well-known that sometimes several -- in several books or in several publications you find the same mistakes because it's not unusual that sometimes people copy what others have written. So therefore, it needs an evaluation. The text, which is published in this book, is in the record. We'll consider that in the totality of all the evidence we will receive in this respect. Mr. Harmon, unless you would insist on that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would agree it should not be in evidence. You will agree as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm satisfied if it's not in evidence. The substance of it was put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the Chamber will think otherwise, you will hear from us tomorrow. We've got a couple of minutes left which is, of course, for Mr. Poplasen not -- perhaps if the interpreters would not -- could we have some seven or eight minutes, because putting one question to a witness and then saying that's it for today is perhaps not a very polite way, and I will explain to the witness that we are a bit late. Madam Usher, could you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The only comment I would make, we have got plenty of time tomorrow. That's the only comment I would make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that's not much consolation for the witness who has waited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, I again have to apologise that you had to wait for some time. We had to deal with a few other procedural matters. We'll not be in this courtroom very long today. I know that it's not a situation you would wish to be in, to wait for such a long time and then to be perhaps only for another ten minutes in court, but we'll continue tomorrow. Mr. Harmon, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, if you would kindly turn to tab 37 in the package of materials before you. Mr. Poplasen, this is a document dated the 9th of September, 1991, from the Serbian Democratic Party, Bosnia-Herzegovina Executive Board, and it is a decision on the appointment of the Commission for Information and Propaganda. It lists 18 people. Your name is found at number 14, and the decision was effective the date that it was adopted. Now, you did in fact serve on this Commission for Information and Propaganda, did you not, Mr. Poplasen?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is the first time I've seen this decision. It doesn't mean it's a forgery, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you serve on a committee that dealt with mass communications and information?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have had to attend at least one meeting of that commission, the constituent meeting. But I never did so. This is the first time I've seen that I was a member of that commission. I assume this was a proposal. Number 1 is an acquaintance and friend of mine, so he probably put forward my name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, whether it's a proposal or not doesn't appear from the text. But the answer is simple: You never served on a committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can I have an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 37, Your Honours, is P1085.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could turn next, Mr. Poplasen, to tab 38. Mr. Poplasen, these tab 38, these are minutes that are from the Serbian Democratic Party for Bosnia and Herzegovina Committee for Mass Communications. It's dated the 8th of October, 1991, and it is the minutes of the first meeting of the Committee for Mass Communications held on 8 August 1991 at the premises of the Delegates' Club between 1800 and 2100 hours. It lists as the people who are present, it lists yourself, it lists Mr. Toholj -- I have not done a comparison of the names to the previous document, but bear with me for just a minute and I will. It also has attending Mr. Miroslav Radovanovic, who was found in the previous document at number 3; it lists Mr. Toholj as present, who is found at the previous document at number 1; it lists Mr. Ostojic as present, who is found in the previous document in number 2; it lists Ilija Guzina as present, he is found in the previous document at number 4; it lists a person whose surname is Nikolic, there's a person bearing the name Nikolic in item number 13; it lists Risto Djogo, whose name -- being present at that meeting, whose name appears in the previous document at number 9. And then it says -- lists a number of people who are absent. It includes Milan Zoric, who is -- appears item number 5 in the previous exhibit; Branislav Lalevic, whose name appears in the previous exhibit at number 7; Dubravka Kenic, whose name appears in the previous document at number 8; Snezana Rakocevic, whose name appears in the previous document at number 10; Ljubo Grkovic, whose name appears at number 12; Kolja Besarovic, whose name appears in the previous document at 15; and finally, Marica Lalovic, whose name appears at number 18. So it appears that the meeting that I'm referring to that is minuted in tab 38 appears to be substantially all of the members who had been named to the Committee on Information and Propaganda. Does this document, Mr. Poplasen, refresh your recollection as to attending such a meeting or appearing in a meeting at which mass communications were discussed within the Republika Srpska? Does this refresh your recollection at all?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to repeat: I have just learnt for the first time that I was a member of the commission you are referring to. Of course I don't remember this meeting at all. It doesn't mean that I wouldn't agree with the contents of the document, but I never attended any meeting of the Commission on Information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That answers Mr. Harmon's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me just -- I'm going to try to refresh your recollection, Mr. Poplasen. At this meeting that I've described, Mr. Karadzic was present and Mr. Krajisnik was also present. At this meeting there was a discussion about the formation of an agency to broadcast what is said in this document "our news." It would function as part of Javnost and it said: "During this year we will try to establish a daily paper, Javnost." This -- these minutes also reflect that the editorial office should send information lasting five minutes to Belgrade TV News on a daily basis in order to achieve a double effect since Belgrade TV News are broadcast here every other day. And it finally ends with a conclusion that it's necessary to form a daily paper, Javnost, as soon as possible. Now, Mr. Poplasen, let me just ask you: Those matters that I have read to you, do those refresh your recollection at all as to attending such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I'm almost sure that this document is a forgery, although all the positions you mention are something I espouse, and had I been there I would have agreed to them, but I'm sure I would have remembered if I had attended such a meeting. I don't know why this is in here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you able to point to anything in the document itself which would suggest that this is a forgery?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, the witness has been confronted with this document for the first time in his life. It's a how-many-page document. We should then give him an opportunity to read it or give him a copy and an opportunity to look at it overnight so he could find this fair to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. We'll make a copy available to the witness, Your Honour, in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm not sure how much more time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the clock. Is there -- would this be a suitable moment to stop?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It will be, Your Honour, because we're going to have to resolve the issue of this document and making one available --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I was actually composing an e-mail as I sit here but I'll put it on the record. The provenance of both these last two tabs is clearly yet to be required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time I think that you will agree that the witness gets a copy of the B/C/S versions of the last documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Your Honour. I agree entirely, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Poplasen, we'll finish for today. You'll be provided with a copy of the minutes of this meeting. Since you expressed the possibility that it could be a forgery, you're invited to tell us whether there's anything in this document which would support your suspicion that it might be a forgery. And please keep in mind there are two types of forgeries: One type is that the document is produced by not at that time, not by the person so said that they produced it; that's one type of forgery. Another type of forgery is that it was produced at the time by the persons mentioned, but that the content does not reflect reality. So when we are talking about forgery, please keep in mind that it could be either of the two, and would you please be so kind as to look at the documents overnight and tell us whether there's anything that -- yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have two documents, both the decision and the minutes of the meeting, which I'll tender right now and give to the witness through the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I noticed, Mr. Harmon, that the minutes are in some respects difficult to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could produce a copy which is better legible, but from the translation I do understand that there might not be a copy which is much better. So you're not blamed, Mr. Poplasen, for not being able to read portions of it, but please concentrate on what you can read. Yes. Then I again would like to instruct you not to speak with anyone about your testimony already given or still to be given. We hope to finish your testimony tomorrow, and we are confident that we'll be able to do so. We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, but not after having thanked the interpreters and the technicians. And we'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 10th day of March, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.
